title: Tracing Inheritance with DNA Markers
endLine: Distinguishable DNA alleles trace genetic parentage and each inherited chromosome.

scenes.tts: Who really fathered a chick, or passed an extra chromosome to a child? Watching birds feed a chick cannot prove genetic parentage. Counting chromosomes alone misses which parent or division erred. DNA markers answer both.
scenes.caption: Who really fathered a chick, or passed an extra chromosome to a child? Watching birds feed a chick cannot prove genetic parentage. Counting chromosomes alone misses which parent or division erred. DNA markers answer both.
scenes.visual: Open directly on the carried Inheritance Board (schematic), filling most of the frame. Top left: two schematic birds feeding a chick, with a bright question mark pulsing over the father. Top right: schematic chromosome bars passing an extra copy into a child slot, also marked with a question mark. Below both, grey marker bands on the chromosomes brighten into distinct colours as the narrator names DNA markers.
scenes.narration: Who really fathered a chick, or passed an extra chromosome to a child? Watching birds feed a chick cannot prove genetic parentage. Counting chromosomes alone misses which parent or division erred. DNA markers answer both.

scenes.visual: The carried Inheritance Board (schematic) softens gently in the background while the title 'Tracing Inheritance with DNA Markers' appears cleanly at full contrast, then dissolves back into the active board.

scenes.tts: A locus is a place on a chromosome, and its versions are alleles. At microsatellite loci, short repeated stretches of DNA vary between individuals. When parents carry distinguishable alleles at a locus, it forms an informative DNA marker. Suppose a father carries alleles one and two, and a mother carries three and four.
scenes.caption: A locus is a place on a chromosome, and its versions are alleles. At microsatellite loci, short repeated stretches of DNA vary between individuals. When parents carry distinguishable alleles at a locus, it forms an informative DNA marker. Suppose a father carries alleles 1 and 2, and a mother carries 3 and 4.
scenes.visual: On the carried Inheritance Board (schematic), zoom onto two parental chromosome pairs—Father left, Mother right. A marker locus lights up on each chromosome bar before the narrator names it, then expands into schematic short repeated blocks of differing lengths (no molecular structures). The blocks resolve into distinct coloured allele bands: Father labelled 1 and 2, Mother labelled 3 and 4.
scenes.narration: A locus is a place on a chromosome, and its versions are alleles. At microsatellite loci, short repeated stretches of DNA vary between individuals. When parents carry distinguishable alleles at a locus, it forms an informative DNA marker. Suppose a father carries alleles 1 and 2, and a mother carries 3 and 4.

scenes.tts: Now put that marker tightly linked to the chromosome twenty-one centromere. Before division, each paired chromosome, or homologue, duplicates into sister copies joined at the centromere. Near the centromere, homologues can carry different alleles, while sister copies usually match. Distinguishable DNA alleles trace genetic parentage and each inherited chromosome.
scenes.caption: Now put that marker tightly linked to the chromosome 21 centromere. Before division, each paired chromosome, or homologue, duplicates into sister copies joined at the centromere. Near the centromere, homologues can carry different alleles, while sister copies usually match. Distinguishable DNA alleles trace genetic parentage and each inherited chromosome.
scenes.visual: On the same Board (schematic), a bright centromere pinch forms on each chromosome 21 bar and the coloured marker band slides right beside it. Each chromosome smoothly duplicates into joined sister copies: Father shows 1-1 and 2-2, Mother shows 3-3 and 4-4. A gentle highlight contrasts Mother's differing homologues (3 versus 4) with her matching sister copies (3-3 and 4-4) as the guiding idea is spoken.

scenes.tts: Test this rule on Child A. The father carries alleles one and two, and the mother carries three and four. Child A inherits alleles one, three, and four. Which parent supplied the extra chromosome, and which classical division failed?
scenes.caption: Test this rule on Child A. The father carries alleles 1 and 2, and the mother carries 3 and 4. Child A inherits alleles 1, 3, and 4. Which parent supplied the extra chromosome, and which classical division failed?
scenes.visual: On the same Board (schematic), Father (1, 2) and Mother (3, 4) remain at top while three chromosome 21 bars glide down into the Child A slot below, settling with bright marker bands labelled 1, 3, and 4. A high-contrast question prompt appears beside Child A: 'Which parent? Which division?'
scenes.narration: Test this rule on Child A. The father carries alleles 1 and 2, and the mother carries 3 and 4. Child A inherits alleles 1, 3, and 4. Which parent supplied the extra chromosome, and which classical division failed?

scenes.visual: Hold the Inheritance Board (schematic) and the question prompt on screen through the thinking pause: Father (1, 2), Mother (3, 4), Child A (1, 3, 4). A subtle progress arc sweeps steadily around the question prompt so the frame stays gently in motion without revealing the answer.

scenes.tts: Trace each allele back. Allele one comes from the father, while alleles three and four come from the mother. So the mother supplied the extra chromosome. Meiosis one parts homologues, and meiosis two parts sisters. Receiving both three and four means the mother's homologues failed to part, a meiosis one error.
scenes.caption: Trace each allele back. Allele 1 comes from the father, while alleles 3 and 4 come from the mother. So the mother supplied the extra chromosome. Meiosis I parts homologues, and meiosis II parts sisters. Receiving both 3 and 4 means the mother's homologues failed to part, a meiosis I error.
scenes.visual: On the Board (schematic), a trace line draws from Child A's allele 1 up to Father, then two trace lines connect alleles 3 and 4 up to Mother as the label 'Mother' lights up. Two short labels appear side by side: 'Meiosis I: homologues part' and 'Meiosis II: sisters part'. Mother's two homologous chromosomes (3-3 and 4-4) stay paired instead of parting during schematic meiosis I, passing both 3 and 4 into the egg; the label 'Meiosis I' settles cleanly.
scenes.narration: Trace each allele back. Allele 1 comes from the father, while alleles 3 and 4 come from the mother. So the mother supplied the extra chromosome. Meiosis I parts homologues, and meiosis II parts sisters. Receiving both 3 and 4 means the mother's homologues failed to part, a meiosis I error.

scenes.tts: One condition can mislead this test. A crossover exchanges segments between two non-sister chromatids in meiosis. Between marker and centromere, that exchange can make sister copies differ. Then meiosis two can resemble meiosis one, and the reverse. Markers close to the centromere reduce that risk. Human eggs also make error patterns beyond the classical two-step model.
scenes.caption: One condition can mislead this test. A crossover exchanges segments between two non-sister chromatids in meiosis. Between marker and centromere, that exchange can make sister copies differ. Then meiosis II can resemble meiosis I, and the reverse. Markers close to the centromere reduce that risk. Human eggs also make error patterns beyond the classical two-step model.
scenes.visual: On the Board (schematic), slide the marker band away from Mother's centromere. Two non-sister chromatids cross between centromere and marker, exchanging coloured tips so one chromosome now carries 3 on one sister and 4 on the other. A caution tag reads 'Meiosis II mimics I'. Then slide the marker tight against the centromere, shrinking the crossover gap and restoring matching sisters, with a brief note that human eggs go beyond the classical two-step model.
scenes.narration: One condition can mislead this test. A crossover exchanges segments between two non-sister chromatids in meiosis. Between marker and centromere, that exchange can make sister copies differ. Then meiosis II can resemble meiosis I, and the reverse. Markers close to the centromere reduce that risk. Human eggs also make error patterns beyond the classical two-step model.

scenes.tts: DNA markers also tested wild parentage on Daphne Major. In 2001, Keller, Grant, Grant and Petren typed birds at eight microsatellite loci. Twenty percent of offspring in their sample were extra-pair young. Their social father was not the genetic father. In this study, pairing chicks with fathers who were not theirs made traits look less inherited than they are.

scenes.visual: The carried Board transitions smoothly to a schematic Daphne Major bird family (Father, Mother, Chick) above an eight-locus microsatellite readout strip (schematic), tagged 'Keller, Grant, Grant and Petren, 2001'. Mismatched bands flash between a chick and the social father feeding it; a schematic gauge highlights twenty percent extra-pair young while a schematic parent-offspring slope tilts flatter under wrong fathers.
scenes.narration: DNA markers also tested wild parentage on Daphne Major. In 2001, Keller, Grant, Grant and Petren typed birds at eight microsatellite loci. Twenty percent of offspring in their sample were extra-pair young. Their social father was not the genetic father. In this study, pairing chicks with fathers who were not theirs made traits look less inherited than they are.

scenes.tts: Even after DNA checked parentage, chicks still resembled their mothers more than their fathers. The authors read that pattern as maternal effects, influences beyond genes like egg size or food. A maternal effect tracking the mother's trait can make inheritance look stronger than it is.
scenes.caption: Even after DNA checked parentage, chicks still resembled their mothers more than their fathers. The authors read that pattern as maternal effects, influences beyond genes like egg size or food. A maternal effect tracking the mother's trait can make inheritance look stronger than it is.
scenes.visual: On the same schematic Daphne Major panel, the genetic father's marker bands now match, yet a glowing link stays stronger between Mother and Chick than between Father and Chick. Schematic icons for egg and food drift from Mother to Chick as the schematic resemblance slope tilts steeper, labelled 'Maternal effects'.

scenes.tts: Alongside wild parentage, centromere-linked markers track extra copies of chromosome twenty-one. They identify which parent supplied the extra chromosome and which classical division failed. Wherever parental alleles differ, reading those DNA tags reveals who passed each chromosome copy.
scenes.caption: Alongside wild parentage, centromere-linked markers track extra copies of chromosome 21. They identify which parent supplied the extra chromosome and which classical division failed. Wherever parental alleles differ, reading those DNA tags reveals who passed each chromosome copy.
scenes.visual: The carried Board brings both views together cleanly (schematic): left, the Daphne Major microsatellite strip matching true genetic parents; right, chromosome 21 centromere markers tracing an extra copy's parent and division. Both panels unify into glowing parental allele tags flowing into offspring chromosomes.
scenes.narration: Alongside wild parentage, centromere-linked markers track extra copies of chromosome 21. They identify which parent supplied the extra chromosome and which classical division failed. Wherever parental alleles differ, reading those DNA tags reveals who passed each chromosome copy.

scenes.visual: Clean high-contrast end card over the softly dimmed Inheritance Board (schematic), displaying the take-home rule in large clear text: 'Distinguishable DNA alleles trace genetic parentage and each inherited chromosome.'
